evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2024: annual hours U.S. adults spend on health care time and paperwork
evidence_cards.unit: hours per year per adult (mean over adults with a valid answer), or percent of adults
evidence_cards.definition: Edited annual hours adults report spending on their own visits and prescriptions, on others' visits, on medical bills and insurance, and on health care paperwork; plus the share who cared for a friend or family member in the past 30 days. Reported per week, month or year and converted to hours per year.
evidence_cards.method: Weighted mean (ESAQ person weight ESAQWT24F) with a Taylor-linearised standard error from VARSTR and VARPSU; adults who skipped an item are excluded from that item.
evidence_cards.source_locator: MEPS HC-256 (2024 Full-Year Consolidated): EQMVAM53, EQOVAM53, EQMBAM53, EQPPAM53, EQCARE53, ESAQWT24F
comparability: All U.S. adults who answered the questionnaire, not people with Lyme disease or Long COVID: MEPS cannot identify either condition reliably (AHRQ, 2026-09-24).
Fielded in 2024 only: the questionnaire was funded for that year, so there is no trend and no later update.

Self-reported. MEPS top-coded the annual hours at the 99.5th percentile (Table 13 of the HC-256 documentation: 2,080 hours for own visits, 1,040 for others' visits, 720 for bills, 520 for paperwork), so a few very large values are capped. About 6% of respondents skipped each time item, and MEPS notes that about 20% of those who completed the paper version gave no answer to them.
Hours, not dollars. Converting hours to dollars needs a published wage or value-of-time source shown next to the estimate.

scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire study (interviews, themes, discussion) concerns patients recruited from a post-COVID recovery clinic who report symptoms persisting ≥3 months after COVID-19 infection; Lyme disease is never mentioned.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a qualitative interview study of 21 adults receiving care at a single academic medical center's post-COVID recovery clinic, conducted August–September 2022, exploring how Long COVID affected their employment and well-being. Participants described reduced work capacity, job loss or job changes, loss of income, disruptive insurance changes, emotional effects like loss of identity and fear of stigma, and mixed success obtaining workplace accommodations or disability benefits. The study does not quantify costs, wage losses, or healthcare spending itself; it reports themes and illustrative quotations rather than a cost model. Several background statistics on Long COVID's employment/disability burden (e.g., a cited $170 billion lost-wages estimate for 2022) are drawn from other cited studies, not generated by this study's own data.

contextual_issues: Long COVID symptoms (brain fog, fatigue, weakness, headaches/migraines) interfered with work tasks and timeframe/volume of output, described qualitatively without a quantified productivity-loss measure.
Work-life balance strain: effort required for work left little energy for other activities, including attending recommended healthcare appointments, described qualitatively.
Employment status changes: voluntary resignation, job switching to more accommodating roles, and involuntary termination, described qualitatively without counts.
Loss of income from inability to return to work, moving to lower-paying jobs, reduced hours, or loss of overtime/side work, described qualitatively without dollar figures.

Insurance disruption: job loss or change forced some participants onto more expensive, lower-coverage plans, with reset deductibles/out-of-pocket maximums, described qualitatively without dollar figures.
Participants reported 'accumulating debt' due to their Long COVID experience, with no amount, frequency, or proportion of the sample quantified.
Emotional/psychological repercussions: loss of self-identity as a 'provider,' guilt, anxiety, fear of judgment/stigma/retaliation at work, described qualitatively.
Access barriers to coping strategies, employer disability benefits, and workplace accommodations, including experiences of employer resistance, described qualitatively without rates.

Diagnostic/documentation barrier: the document notes there is a 'lack of established practices to diagnose Long COVID,' making it 'challenging' to apply for workplace accommodation without objective diagnostic data, forcing reliance on functional-limitation questionnaires instead.

The introduction cites (but does not itself measure) external estimates for background context: ~25% of a sampled Long COVID population reporting significant activity limitations (cited to ref 2), ~two-thirds reporting a disability (cited to ref 3), lower full-time employment/higher unemployment likelihood relative to those without Long COVID (cited to ref 4), 22% unable to work and 45% requiring reduced schedule at 6 months post-infection (cited to ref 6), 18% unable to return to work at 1 year (cited to ref 7), and a minimum of $170 billion in lost U.S. wages in 2022 (cited to ref 8, Suran/JAMA 2023). These are secondhand citations used to motivate the study, not findings this document itself measured or modeled.
evidence_gaps: No quantification of direct medical costs, direct non-medical costs (travel, paid help), or indirect costs (lost wages, productivity, caregiving time) for this specific sample.
No measure of magnitude or duration of income loss, insurance premium/deductible increases, or debt accumulation reported by participants.

Sample is restricted to patients with access to a single academic post-COVID recovery clinic, likely enriched for more severe/prolonged Long COVID and higher care-seeking motivation; findings may not generalize to milder cases or those without clinic access.
No race/ethnicity data were collected, precluding any demographic cost/burden disaggregation on that dimension for this cohort.
No comparison group (e.g., individuals without Long COVID) was studied, so relative burden cannot be quantified from this document alone.
No longitudinal follow-up; the study is a single cross-sectional set of interviews (August–September 2022), so long-term financial trajectories are not captured.
comparison_boundaries: This qualitative N=21 single-clinic sample cannot be pooled with population-level quantitative estimates mentioned in the introduction (e.g., the $170 billion 2022 lost-wages figure, or the 22%/45%/18% employment-status percentages) because those come from different studies, different populations (e.g., national workers' compensation claims, international cohort surveys), different time windows, and different measurement methods (survey/claims-based vs. qualitative interview).

The background statistics cited in the introduction (ref 2 activity-limitation percentage, ref 3 disability percentage, ref 4 employment-likelihood comparison, ref 6 6-month work-capacity percentages, ref 7 1-year return-to-work percentage, ref 8 lost-wages estimate) are themselves drawn from separate source studies with different populations and time horizons and should not be merged into a single burden figure.

Participant characteristics (e.g., 76% female, mean age 47.6, enrollment skewed toward those with Long COVID lasting >1 year) describe this specific sample only and must not be generalized as the demographic profile of the broader Long COVID population.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document describes a regulatory/clinical-practice gap: there is a 'lack of established practices to diagnose Long COVID,' making it difficult for clinicians and patients to support workplace accommodation requests without objective diagnostic data, requiring reliance on functional-limitation questionnaires instead of diagnostic testing.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Discussion section: 'Due to lack of established practices to diagnose Long COVID, it is important to recognize the challenge of applying for work accommodation without objective diagnostic data. Accommodations can be requested based on documented functional limitations, rather than diagnostic testing.'

decision_relevance.summary: This qualitative study could inform post-COVID care teams, patient advocates, and policy audiences about the lived, non-quantified dimensions of Long COVID's employment and financial impact — job loss, insurance disruption, debt, emotional toll, and accommodation barriers — that a cost simulator must represent as themes/scenarios rather than dollar inputs, since the document itself supplies no cost figures. It is most useful for designing qualitative decision-support content (e.g., what financial/emotional risks to screen for) rather than for parameterizing a quantitative cost model.
use_cases: Post-COVID clinic care teams could use the identified themes (loss of income, insurance changes, debt, fear of workplace stigma) to build a structured screening checklist that triggers referral to financial navigators, mental health treatment, or disability-documentation support.

Patient/advocate-facing content could use the qualitative accounts of insurance disruption and diagnostic-documentation barriers to help patients anticipate and prepare for workplace accommodation or disability-benefit conversations with their care team, while being clear this is lived-experience evidence, not a population cost estimate.

No comparison group (e.g., individuals without Long COVID) was studied, so relative burden cannot be quantified from this document alone.
No longitudinal follow-up; the study is a single cross-sectional set of interviews (August–September 2022), so long-term financial trajectories are not captured.

package.documentation:
## What this tool represents
The underlying document is a qualitative interview study of 21 adults receiving care at a single academic post-COVID recovery clinic, interviewed August–September 2022, exploring how Long COVID affected employment and well-being. Participants described reduced work capacity, job loss or change, income loss, disruptive insurance changes, debt, and emotional effects (loss of identity, fear of stigma), along with mixed success obtaining accommodations or disability benefits. The study reports themes and illustrative quotations; it does not itself quantify costs, wages, or healthcare spending for its own participants.

## Where the numbers come from
Because this study has no cost data of its own, every percentage and dollar figure in this simulator except the two plainly-labeled assumptions (the annual wage and the reduced-schedule income fraction) is a statistic the document's introduction cites from separate external studies (different populations and methods): a 22% unable-to-work and 45% reduced-schedule rate at 6 months post-infection (ref 6), an 18% unable-to-return rate at 1 year (ref 7), and a minimum $170 billion 2022 national lost-wages estimate (ref 8, Suran/JAMA 2023). These external figures describe different cohorts than this study's 21 participants and should not be pooled with, or treated as evidence about, this specific clinic sample. The illustrative income-loss outputs combine these cited external shares with an assumed annual wage purely to show the rough scale of possible income loss; they are not a cost estimate this study produced or validated.

## Limitation: diagnostic/documentation gap
The document describes a systemic limitation: there is no established practice to diagnose Long COVID, which made it difficult for participants to support workplace accommodation requests with objective diagnostic data. Instead, accommodations had to be requested based on documented functional limitations rather than diagnostic testing - a gap in clinical/regulatory practice, not a measurement issue with this study's burden estimate.

## Other limitations
The sample is restricted to one academic clinic's patients, likely enriched for more severe or prolonged Long COVID; no race/ethnicity data were collected; there is no comparison group of people without Long COVID; and the design is a single cross-sectional set of interviews, so long-term financial trajectories were not tracked. Participant characteristics (76% female, mean age 47.6) describe this sample only and should not be generalized.
